Fatigue and depression in MS overlap on every questionnaire that tries to tell
them apart. Effort-based decision making offers a behavioural separation:
whether the cost of action or the value of the outcome is what has changed.

## Where the overlap comes from {.k-head}

Some of it is built into the instruments. Zaehle and Linnhoff compared two
versions of the same depression inventory in MS. The full Beck Depression
Inventory asks about tiredness, sleep and lost energy; its fast-screen form
drops those items and keeps the mood ones. The correlation with fatigue was
weaker on the shorter scale. Part of the link between fatigue and depression is
two scales asking the same question and counting the answer twice.

The rest is not a measurement artefact. Sparasci and colleagues assessed
fatigue, sleepiness and depression with objective tools as well as
questionnaires and still could not pull them apart. Chang and colleagues, in the
FutureMS cohort of newly diagnosed patients, mapped the symptoms as a network
and found fatigue attaching to particular depressive items rather than to
depression as a whole.

Enoka and colleagues argue that some of the confusion is a word. Fatigue is what
a person reports feeling. Fatigability is the measurable decline in performance
as a task goes on. The two track each other poorly, and a literature that uses
one term for both will keep discovering overlaps it created itself.

## What effort-based decision making measures {.k-head}

The framework treats motivation as arithmetic. How much is the outcome worth,
how much does getting it cost, and is the difference positive. A person is
offered the same choice many times, a small reward for little work against a
larger one for more, with the amounts varied. What comes out is the exchange
rate between the two.

This is worth doing because "I cannot get started" has at least two solutions.
The reward may have stopped being worth anything, which is what anhedonia
describes. Or the reward may be intact and the action have become expensive.
Both produce the same sentence in clinic and different curves on the task.

Husain and Roiser set out the case for reading apathy and anhedonia this way
across diagnoses rather than inside one. The separation has since been shown
directly in several diseases. Le Heron and colleagues found apathy and dopamine
to have distinct effects on effort-based choice in Parkinson's disease. Saleh
and colleagues, in small vessel cerebrovascular disease, pulled apathy and
depression apart on different parameters of the same decision. Blouzard and
colleagues pooled the schizophrenia studies and found a consistent reduction in
willingness to work for reward.

## What has been tried in MS {.k-head}

Erani and colleagues ran the closest thing to this question. Forty patients and
forty matched controls did a switching task with effort and reward varied
independently, rating their fatigue as they went. Effort raised reported fatigue
and reward improved performance, but the interaction between them, which is what
the effort-reward account predicts, did not appear. The authors' own reading is
that the reward manipulation may not have been salient enough to produce it.

Müller and colleagues complicate the picture from another direction. Modelling
two effort-based tasks, they found that willingness to work is not a fixed
quantity: two hidden states of fatigue build up on different timescales, one
recoverable by rest and one not, and both lower the value of effort. A single
number for how effort-averse someone is may be averaging over something that
moves while you measure it.

Bogdanov and colleagues review the paradigms and find they differ enough,
physical against cognitive effort, choice before against after exertion, demand
stated against demand learned, that results do not transfer freely between them.
Which task is used is part of the finding.

So the question this project asks is open rather than answered, and the one
attempt at it in MS was null. Data collection is running. Nothing is claimed
here about what it will show.
